content: Individuals with fragile X syndrome have been hypothesized to exhibit low levels of folate in their bodies, and it has been suggested that dietary supplementation with folic acid might alleviate the developmental and behavioral challenges associated with the condition. To evaluate this hypothesis, a systematic review was conducted to assess the efficacy and safety of folic acid treatment in individuals with fragile X syndrome. The review included randomized controlled trials identified through searches of four databases—CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, and PsycINFO—conducted in November 2010. Five trials, published between 1986 and 1992, met the inclusion criteria. These studies collectively involved 67 male participants, ranging in age from 1 to 54 years. The intellectual disabilities of the participants varied from borderline to severe, and some individuals were also diagnosed with autism or exhibited autistic behaviors. Four of the studies employed a placebo-controlled crossover design, while one used a parallel design. The duration of follow-up ranged from two to twelve months, with treatment or placebo periods lasting between two and eight months. Folic acid doses varied from 10 mg to 250 mg per day, with 10 mg per day being the most commonly administered dose. Many of the younger participants were concurrently enrolled in special education programs, which typically included language and occupational therapy. The review did not allow for a meta-analysis due to the heterogeneity of the studies. None of the individual trials demonstrated evidence of clinical benefit from folic acid treatment in fragile X syndrome patients. Specifically, no improvements were observed in psychological or learning abilities, behavior, or social performance, as assessed using standardized measurement tools. When the data were analyzed separately for prepubertal children and postpubertal young individuals, some statistically significant findings were noted. However, these results did not provide clear evidence of benefit for either age group. Adverse effects associated with folic acid treatment were infrequent, mild, and transient. However, the overall quality of the studies was poor, with only one trial classified as having a low risk of bias. The small sample sizes and methodological limitations of the included studies reduced their statistical power, making it unlikely that they could detect anything other than very large treatment effects. In conclusion, the available evidence regarding the use of folic acid in individuals with fragile X syndrome is of low quality and insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about its efficacy or safety. Further research with larger, well-designed trials is necessary to determine whether folic acid supplementation has any meaningful impact on this population.
